name: template-view
intent: Render a mostly static markup document that contains markers, resolving each marker from a prepared view model at render time, so presentation lives in an editable artifact instead of in string-building code.
problem: A response is fixed markup except for the few values that vary per request, but the page is produced by concatenating strings in program code: markup authors cannot touch it, indentation and quoting are lost in the concatenation, escaping is re-decided at every insertion point, and each layout change ripples through the code that emits it. The recurring decision is how the static text and the dynamic values are combined.
context: Server-side presentation where the output is a text document - HTML, XML, CSV, an email body, a report, the HTML behind a PDF - that is mostly static with holes to fill. It applies when presentation should be editable as a document (designers, translators, non-programmers), when the same chrome repeats across pages, and when escaping must be uniform; it assumes the model can be prepared before rendering and that no second presentation stage (a logical screen, a per-channel renderer) is needed.
benefits: The page becomes an editable document: indentation, ordering and surrounding markup survive editing, so markup authors change presentation without touching or rebuilding program code.
Escaping is decided once by the engine for the context a value lands in, instead of being re-decided at every string-concatenation site.
Repeated chrome has a single home: layouts, blocks and partials remove the duplicated header/nav/footer that programmatic page building accumulates.
Separation of concerns holds: the view code prepares a model and selects a template, the template places values, and the two change for different reasons.
One mechanism covers every text format - an HTML page, an XML feed, a CSV export, an email body, a configuration file - differing only in the template, not in the rendering machinery.
Templates become assets: they can be syntax-highlighted, linted, cached or precompiled, and rendered output can be diffed against a golden file.
tradeoffs: Marker/model coupling is discovered late: the template names values the view must supply, and outside compile-time engines (Twirl, Razor, Askama) a renamed or missing field shows up as an empty region or a render error on the request path.

Logic pressure: the first conditional or loop either grows a second programming language inside the markup or forces the model to be pre-shaped in code; both costs are real, and a genuinely data-driven page degrades into Template Script.

Escaping is only as good as its context handling: the engine escapes for the position it understands, so values placed into JavaScript, CSS, URL or attribute contexts - and every raw/safe marker - reopen injection holes.
Rendering costs parse-and-render work per request unless compiled templates are cached; escaping, whitespace handling and control tags add CPU and output noise to every page.

Tooling is weaker than for code: template errors surface late, stack traces cross the engine's internals, and tests tend to assert on rendered strings, which is brittle compared with asserting on data.

It is the wrong output shape for machine consumers: when the payload must be negotiated, validated or consumed as data, a programmatic view or a serializer keeps the logic and the tests in the language's own tooling.

participants.responsibility: The markup document holding the static text and the markers that identify where model values belong; it is the primary artifact and the unit the markup author edits.
Parses the template once or per request, resolves markers against the model, escapes each value for the context it is inserted into, and writes the rendered output.
The prepared data the markers resolve against - shaped for presentation by the view code instead of being a raw domain object graph.
Chooses the template for the request, assembles the view model, hands both to the engine and passes the rendered result to the response.
Shared fragments - chrome, navigation, forms, repeated blocks - that templates extend or include so the same markup is not repeated per page.

use_cases: Server-rendered HTML pages in a web application, where the route or controller prepares the model and the template owns the markup.
Transactional and marketing email bodies: HTML documents with per-recipient values and a shared layout fragment.
Document and report generation - invoices, statements, HTML rendered to PDF, configuration files, code and data exports - from the same template mechanism.
Static-site and documentation generators that merge content with a shared layout at build time.
Internationalised pages where the surrounding markup is stable and the localised strings and per-locale formatting are the values that change.
Admin and internal-tool screens whose markup is largely boilerplate with a few tables and fields filled from the model.

Go's html/template package: server-rendered HTML pages where {{.Field}} markers resolve against a supplied data structure and the engine escapes every value for the context it lands in - HTML, CSS, JavaScript or URL - instead of at the call site.

Play Framework's Twirl templates: .scala.html files compile to Scala functions at build time, so a marker naming a missing or renamed model field fails the build rather than rendering an empty region on the first request.

ASP.NET Core Razor Pages: each .cshtml page pairs with a PageModel class that handles the request and prepares the model while the Razor view places @-model values into mostly static markup - the handler/template split the pattern prescribes.
avoid_when: The response is machine-consumed data (a JSON or XML API payload): serialising a typed object is smaller, testable in the language, and free of a second template language.
The output is trivial - one field, one string - and interpolation in the language already states it clearly; an engine and a template file add a dependency and a moving part.

The logic genuinely dominates the markup (per-row computation, state-dependent styling, queries while rendering): prepare the data in code and render a programmatic view (Transform View), or extract helpers (View Helper), instead of growing the template into a script.
One model must be rendered into several channels or formats with per-channel decisions: build a logical screen first and render it per channel (Two Step View).
The page is assembled from independently rendered fragments (portals, dashboards, widgets): a composite view over fragment templates fits better than one large template.
Template authors are untrusted (end users may supply templates): most engines execute template code in the host process, so template authorship is a privilege, not a feature.
anti_patterns: "Fat template": business rules, calculations, database access or service calls written into the markup, so the page's behaviour is testable only through the renderer.
Blanket unescaping - every marker wrapped in a raw/safe form (|safe, @Html.Raw, th:utext, <%-) - which reduces the engine's escaping to decoration.
Domain entities passed straight to the template, so lazy-loaded relations, side-effecting methods and internal fields become part of the view surface and N+1 queries become presentation bugs.
Helper objects that fetch data or hold business logic and are invoked from the template: the coupling the pattern removes comes back, hidden in a helper library.
One nearly identical template per state or variation, instead of one template with a model-driven branch or a shared partial, multiplying the markup that must be kept in step.
Templates edited without any render test or golden output, so a renamed field ships as an empty region or a 500 discovered in production.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: markup and logic change for different reasons and live in different artifacts.
Secure defaults at the boundary: escaping belongs to the rendering boundary and stays on by default, with each raw mark a reviewed exception.
Information hiding: the template sees a purpose-built view model, never the persistence or domain internals rendered nearby.
DRY through composition: layouts, blocks and partials give shared chrome and repeated fragments a single home.
Open/closed: a new page adds a template and a route, not edits to the rendering machinery.
Single responsibility per role: the engine renders, the handler models, the template places - none of them does another's job.
best_practices: Keep auto-escaping on and treat every raw/unescaped marker as a review item; frame it as a security decision, not a formatting preference.
Prepare a view model shaped for the page - only the fields the template reads - and resolve collections in the handler so the template never triggers a query.
Keep templates logic-light: iterate pre-computed collections, branch on pre-computed booleans, and move anything a reviewer would want unit-tested back into code.
Give the shared chrome a layout and repeated fragments partials or includes, so a navigation change touches one file.
Compile or cache templates at startup (parse once, render per request; precompile where the engine supports it) and fail fast when a template does not parse.
Test the rendering seam: one golden or snapshot render per template plus assertions on the values that matter, so a marker-to-model rename fails a test instead of a page.
Prefer the engine's contextual escaping helpers (Go's context-aware html/template, Razor's encoders, Twirl's content types) over hand-rolled escaping.
sources: Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002) - Template View (Web Presentation Patterns, chapter 14).
